study_id: Zadeh et al. - 2024 - Predictive analytics for de novo malignancies after lung transplantation

eligibility.Eligibility Rationale: The study analyzes adult lung transplant recipients using non‑linear machine learning models (gradient boosting, neural networks) to predict post‑transplant malignancy, meeting population, intervention, outcome, and study design criteria.

identification_methods.Comments: Predictive analytics study using machine learning to predict de novo malignancies after lung transplantation.
identification_methods.Institution: Department of Information Systems, Raj Soin College of Business, Wright State University
identification_methods.Address: 3640 Colonel Glenn Hwy, Dayton, OH 45435, USA
identification_methods.Dataset Source: Standard Transplant Analysis and Research (STAR) database
identification_methods.Identification Notes: Included lung transplant recipients without prior malignancy; final cohort of 30,917 individuals after exclusions.
identification_methods.AI Model Architecture: Gradient Boosting, Decision Trees, Logistic Regression, Neural Networks, Random Forest, Least Angle Regression (LARS), Support Vector Machine, Rule Induction
identification_methods.Class Imbalance: Oversampling of minority class was applied.
identification_methods.Comparator: Multiple machine learning models were compared; gradient boosting performed best.
identification_methods.Input Variables: Recipient and donor demographics, HLA antigen levels, BMI, CMV status, total serum albumin, intra‑operative data, post‑transplant outcomes, and other clinical variables.
identification_methods.Validation Method: 70% training / 30% testing split; no cross‑validation reported.
identification_methods.Methods Notes: Data cleaning and preprocessing performed in SAS Enterprise Miner; expert review removed irrelevant/redundant variables; 544 initial variables reduced to 371 after exclusion of 173; models trained on balanced data with oversampling.

population.Exclusion criteria: Recipients with documented history of malignant cancer were excluded
population.Population Notes: Data extracted from the STAR database; only lung transplants included; final cohort of 30,917 individuals with 25% developing post‑transplant malignancy

interventions_outcomes.Intervention Input Data Modality: Tabular clinical variables from the STAR transplant registry (pre-, during-, and post‑transplant measures)
interventions_outcomes.Number of Predictors: 371 predictors (after excluding 173 of the original 544 variables)
interventions_outcomes.Feature Selection Method: Variable importance ranking by gradient boosting combined with expert review
interventions_outcomes.Temporal Handling: Static baseline model using longitudinal variables aggregated into a single feature set
interventions_outcomes.Interventions Notes: Gradient boosting configured with 50 iterations, shrinkage factor 0.1, trained on 60% of observations; oversampling used for class imbalance
interventions_outcomes.Reported outcomes in study: Prediction of de novo malignancy after lung transplantation; performance metrics include AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity
interventions_outcomes.Outcomes Notes: Primary outcome is binary occurrence of post‑transplant malignancy
interventions_outcomes.Result data Notes: Gradient boosting achieved the highest AUC (0.746) among all models evaluated
interventions_outcomes.Primary Outcome Reported against: Other machine‑learning models (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, decision tree)
interventions_outcomes.Primary Outcome Metric Definition: AUC calculated on a held‑out test set (30% of the data)
interventions_outcomes.Primary Outcome Notes: Gradient boosting outperformed all other models with AUC 0.746; key predictive variables included DR52 antigen, BMI, CMV IgG status, and total serum albumin
